title: Narada and the guardians' halls
hookLine: Yudhishthira asks Narada if he's ever seen a hall like this, and Narada describes the halls of the gods
carry: lokapalas: every direction has a guardian

lines: HAVE YOU SEEN A HALL LIKE THIS?
cards: It's a very human question. The questions are over, the king has promised to do better, and then Yudhishthira asks Narada something else. You've traveled through every world, he says.
Have you ever seen a hall like this one, or a better one? He's sitting in the hall Maya built; of course he wants to know. And Narada's answer is careful.
Among humans, he says, never. But there are other halls.

teach.b: Then Narada describes them, one after another, the halls of the gods. The hall of Indra, king of the gods. Of Yama, lord of the dead.
Of Varuna, out among the waters. Of Kubera, lord of wealth. And the hall of Brahma, the creator, which Narada says can't be properly described at all, because its form keeps changing.
Listen to how he describes them. He tells what they're made of and how bright they are, but mostly he lists who sits there: sages, kings of old, ancestors, rivers and mountains in person.

teach.h: EACH HALL KNOWN BY WHO SITS THERE.
teach.b: Each hall is known by its gathering, the word sabha again. And notice whose halls these are.

teach.h: LOKAPALAS: A GUARDIAN FOR EACH DIRECTION.
teach.b: Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera: in Hindu tradition they're lokapalas, guardians of the world, and each keeps a direction. Indra the east, where the sun rises. Yama the south.
Varuna the west. Kubera the north. That's why some Hindu temples carve them on their outer walls, facing their directions: the holy place stands inside a world watched on every side.
So Narada's answer doesn't flatter Yudhishthira, and it doesn't scold him.
Nothing among humans matches your hall, he says, and then shows him the larger world it stands in, guarded in every direction, and beyond it a hall no words can hold.

teach.h: NOTHING LIKE IT ON EARTH. HERE IS THE SKY.
teach.b: Many teachers read it as a gentle lesson in humility. It's also a setup. In Yama's hall, among the kings who've died, is someone Yudhishthira would know.

how: In Hindu tradition, Indra (east), Yama (south), Varuna (west) and Kubera (north) are among the guardians of the directions, the lokapalas or dikpalas, and their images are carved at their directions on the walls of some temples.

o: a hall, known by the assembly that sits in it
the heaven where the gods live forever
a temple built for one particular god

games.q: the guardians of the directions — tap the pairs.

s: Narada told Yudhishthira his hall was nothing special
he said that among humans he had never seen its like.
Narada describes the halls mostly by who sits in them
sages, kings of old, ancestors: each hall is known by its gathering.
Narada gave a full description of Brahma's hall
he says it can't be properly described, because its form keeps changing.

games.q: you're Narada. a king in a magnificent hall asks if you've ever seen a better one. what do you say?
o: flatter him: no hall anywhere compares.
say that among humans none, then describe the halls of the gods.
tell him pride in buildings is foolish.
games.why: he doesn't flatter and doesn't scold. he says nothing on earth compares, then opens the frame to the halls of the gods.

practice: If you can, stand and turn slowly to each direction: east, south, west, north. In each one, think of what lies that way, a street, a city, someone you love. Some Hindu prayers greet each direction in turn.
If you pray, ask God to watch over that side of your world; if you don't, simply notice that your room sits inside something much bigger, on every side.

wordCard.voice: Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, Narada's tour of the halls of the gods, the guardians of the directions, each hall known by who sits in it.

orig.note: Sanskrit lokapāla: a guardian of the world. Indra, Yama, Varuna and Kubera, whose halls Narada describes, are counted among them.

carryVoice: Your line: lokapalas: every direction has a guardian. Narada gave pride company, not a scolding. That's the week.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Lokapala Sabhakhyana Parva (Yudhishthira's question; Narada describes the halls of Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera and Brahma)
